$description: The shared semantic vocabulary — the concepts Market and Move both have, under one name each, resolved per mode. Decision 007 is the rule: a mode answers 'what value does this concept take here?', a namespace answers 'whose concept is this?'. Everything in this file passed the factual test — does the other product have this concept at all? — and everything that failed it lives in commerce.json or mobility.json instead. Thirteen names and two plumbing slots, and the count is deliberate: every shared semantic has to resolve in all four mode combinations, so each name added here is four decisions and four contrast checks, not one. It was eleven until decision 023 added text.error and border.error together — two names for one value, because they are gated at different thresholds and a single name would have had to pick one of them. Every value in this file is a reference. A semantic that restates a literal has stopped naming a decision and become a second copy of it, and machinery/scripts/check-schema.mjs rejects it as semantic-literal.

surface.$description: The grounds. Two of them, which is the minimum that lets a panel sit inside a page and still be seen as a separate plane.

default.$description: The page ground. Base is light, where it is pure white; the dark theme swaps it to neutral.1000. It is the background in eight of the fifteen declared pairs, which makes it the single value most of the system's legibility hangs off. It is also, under the name focus.ring-contrast, the foreground in two more: the light bands of the focus indicator are this value, so a ground here is a mark there, and a change to it is read twice — once as legibility under 1.4.3 and once as an indicator under 1.4.11.

sunken.$description: A panel set into the page — a tinted card body, a filled input, a well. It is checked as a separate background from surface.default rather than assumed to behave like it, because it is the tighter of the two grounds in both themes and it is where text.secondary comes closest to failing.

text.$description: Two neutral text tiers and one inverse, and no more. Decision 009 deleted the muted tier after the arithmetic showed a third step could be declared but not seen; de-emphasis below secondary is now a size and weight job, not a colour job.

primary.$description: Body and heading text. Not black in either theme — neutral.900 on white in light, neutral.0 on neutral.1000 in dark — which leaves 13.39:1 and 18.42:1, both far above the floor, and keeps the page from ringing on a bright screen.

secondary.$description: The second and last neutral text tier. It is the one shared semantic that depends on BOTH dimensions: theme decides how light the ramp runs, product decides which step of it is taken. That is the density refusal from decision 008 kept alive as a mode difference — Market is browsed on a sofa and takes the heavier step, Move is read at a curb in one glance and takes the lighter one. Because a mode file belongs to exactly one dimension and cannot see the other, this token does not name a primitive directly: it aliases whichever of the two per-product slots below applies, and the theme dimension sets the slots. Components reference this name and stay product-agnostic; the slots are plumbing.

secondary-market.$description: PLUMBING, NOT VOCABULARY. Market's secondary text value, resolved by the theme dimension alone: neutral.700 in light (6.90:1 on white), neutral.400 in dark (9.29:1 on neutral.1000). It exists only so that text.secondary can be selected by the product dimension after the theme dimension has already decided the value. No component may reference it — a component that does has become product-aware, which is exactly what decision 007 exists to prevent. Use text.secondary.

secondary-move.$description: PLUMBING, NOT VOCABULARY, on the same terms as text.secondary-market. Move's secondary text value: neutral.650 in light (5.33:1 on white, and 4.76:1 on surface.sunken — the tightest NEUTRAL text pairing in the system, and the tightest of any kind until decision 023 added text.error at 4.73:1 on the same ground in dark) and neutral.500 in dark (6.07:1). The two slots exist as a pair rather than one slot and one inline value, so that neither product's density is the default and the other the exception. Use text.secondary.

on-action.$description: Label text sitting on a filled action. neutral.0 in both themes, because action.primary does not change with the theme — the fill is what carries the contrast, and both brand hues were set at the lightness that lets white sit on them at 4.5:1 (5.64:1 on green.600, 5.27:1 on blue.600). It is stated in both theme files rather than left to inherit, so that a future theme cannot silently invert it.

error.$description: The message that tells a user what they entered is not accepted. A text colour, gated at 4.5:1 on both grounds, and deliberately NOT the same token as border.error even though the two hold identical values in both themes — decision 023 is the argument, and decision 008 is the precedent: status colour and status text are two jobs, and the ambers had to be pulled apart once already for exactly this conflation. It is also not mobility.safety, which is hazard and cancellation *content* and belongs to one product, and not commerce.discount, which is a price treatment that happens to be red. A shared component may reference none of those and needs this one: both products have forms, and a form error is interface feedback rather than anything either product owns. red.600 in light (5.62:1 on surface.default) and red.300 in dark, on the ramp's own light-grounds/dark-grounds split — the polarity flip a text colour needs and a brand fill does not.

action.$description: The primary action and its hover, resolved by product and not by theme. Decision 008's correction is the reason: the two greens that merged were both Market-lineage drift, so the merge was within Market and never across products. Market is green, Move is blue, and the audit was explicit that the two lineages stay independent.

primary.$description: The resting primary action fill. green.600 in Market, blue.600 in Move, and the same value in light and dark — a saturated fill carrying white text does not need the polarity flip a text colour does, and flipping it would make the brand two colours instead of one. This is the single-dimension case: product decides it, theme never touches it.

primary-hover.$description: Hover and pressed on the primary action. The interval between 600 and 700 was set by decision 008 to the size a state change actually has to be — v0's two brand greens were 2.90 ΔE00 apart while a hover needs about 9.23 — and green and blue use the matched interval so a state change feels the same size in either product. Not declared as a pair in pairs.json: text.on-action clears 4.5:1 on the resting fill and both hover steps are darker still, so the resting pair is the binding case.

border.$description: Two line tokens, split by what the line is doing rather than by how heavy it looks. The split is what makes the decorative context in pairs.json defensible: a divider is exempt from WCAG 1.4.11 and a control edge is not, so they cannot be the same token.

default.$description: The 1px neutral hairline — a card outline, a divider between list rows. Declared decorative in pairs.json, so its ratio is measured and printed in all four combinations and nothing gates it: it sits at 1.48:1 in light and 1.70:1 in dark, which is what a divider is supposed to look like. Gating it at 3:1 would force every card edge to roughly neutral.500 and produce a boxed-in interface nobody asked for. The moment a line starts identifying a control, it is border.control.

control.$description: The boundary of an interactive control — an input, a checkbox, an unfilled button. Gated at the 1.4.11 non-text threshold. READ THE VALUE THAT SHIPS, NOT THE ONE DECLARED HERE: the base is neutral.500, but theme.light and theme.dark both override it to neutral.600, so what renders is 4.29:1 in both themes — 1.29 above the 3.0 bar, and identical in all four mode combinations, which is why the build hoists it to the root block. neutral.500 on white would be 3.03:1, and an earlier version of this description called that the tightest gated pair in the system on the strength of the base value alone. It is not. That claim then named text.secondary on surface.sunken in light + Move, at 4.76:1 against a 4.5 bar, and decision 023 has taken the title off it too: the tightest gated pair is now text.error on surface.sunken in dark, at 4.73:1 against the same bar — 0.23 of headroom, and the number to watch if either red or surface.sunken moves. The lesson is that a base value overridden in every mode is not a value the system has — it is a default nothing selects, and describing it as though it renders is the easiest way to be wrong about your own tokens. neutral.500 still exists as the documented floor for a non-text mark on white; this token simply does not sit on it.

error.$description: The edge of a control whose value was not accepted. The third line token, and it splits on the same axis the other two do — what the line is DOING, not how heavy it looks. A divider is exempt from 1.4.11, a control edge is not, and a control edge that is also the error signal is a control edge: gated at 3.0, never at the 4.5 its twin text.error carries. That difference in threshold is the whole reason these are two names for one value rather than one name used twice. The invalid state is drawn with this token and not with a border-width change, because the width scale does not exist (Button.css still writes the one literal 1px in the system) and because a heavier edge alone is not a signal a colour-blind user reads any better — it is the pairing of this edge with the text.error message and aria-invalid that carries the state, never any one of the three by itself. red.600 in light, red.300 in dark, identical to text.error in both and independently tunable by construction.

focus.$description: The two tones of the focus indicator. Neither holds a value of its own — one aliases text.primary and the other surface.default — and the rendered indicator is byte-for-byte what it was before these names existed. That is the argument for them, not against them: the values were never the problem, the ownership was. An indicator is governed by WCAG 1.4.11 and by what it lands on; a text colour and a page ground are governed by 1.4.3 and by how a page reads at length. Those are different constraints with different binding cases, and while they shared two names they were one edit. Two names is what lets the gate print a pairing that says 'focus indicator' and lets a reviewer see an indicator move.

ring.$description: The dark band — the 2px outline the eye actually reads, flanked on both sides by focus.ring-contrast. It borrows text.primary and shares nothing else with it. The alias does not freeze the value: change text.primary a step lighter because headings ring on a bright screen, and this band follows it in the same commit, exactly as it did before. What the alias changes is where that shows up. The pairing the contrast gate prints is 'focus.ring on action.primary', not 'text.primary on action.primary', so the run says an indicator moved rather than that a text colour did; the exception that carries this band at 2.37:1 in light is written against a name that describes what is being excepted; and unbinding the two is a one-line edit at a token that already exists, made on purpose, rather than a fork somebody has to think to create. A shared value is fine. A shared name is what turns a typographic decision into an accessibility one without anybody deciding it.

ring-contrast.$description: The light band, drawn on both sides of focus.ring: 0–2px inside the outline and 4–8px outside it. It borrows surface.default because the two tones have to stay opposite polarities of one axis in both themes — surface.default is white in light and neutral.1000 in dark, the exact reverse of text.primary — and text.on-action, white in both, would have collapsed the pair into one colour in dark. Named -contrast rather than -light or -on-dark because which of the two is lighter is the theme's answer and not the token's: this is the tone whose job is to be unlike the other one, and it holds that job in all four combinations. It is also the tone that touches the world, so it is the one that has to clear 3.0 against whatever the indicator lands on — 5.64:1 and 5.27:1 on the light brand fills, 3.27:1 and 3.50:1 on the dark ones, dark Market binding at 0.27 of headroom — while on surface.sunken it is at 1.12:1 and excepted, because there focus.ring is carrying the indicator instead. Same reason for the name as focus.ring: surface.default is a ground and will move for the reasons grounds move, and this band is gated.
